identity.title: Referencing, Citation and Academic Integrity (academic skills pathway)
identity.agentDefinition: Referencing, Citation and Academic Integrity is one of thirteen academic skills pathways: acknowledging where knowledge comes from, from the mechanics of in-text references and a references list in one consistent style, through quotation, paraphrase and citation as evidence of scope and engagement, to the values of academic integrity as part of graduate and professional identity. Reach for it to place, sequence or assess a referencing or integrity capability, or to translate one into its workplace form; it also carries the managing of sources as they are found. It is not about research ethics in the field, which belongs to Researching, nor about the integrity questions raised by AI tools, which belong to the AI and technology pathway.
identity.summary: The academic skills pathways model (2026) sets Referencing, Citation and Academic Integrity as one of thirteen pathways, drawn from a study skills guide's chapter on academic integrity and referencing. The model reverses the guide's order: the guide opens with integrity and its values and comes to referencing after, while the pathway starts with the mechanics, moves to citation and plagiarism and ends with the values. It climbs in three tiers: getting referencing right (why we reference, in-text references and the references list, author-date mechanics for the common source types, accuracy and consistency, copy-paste errors, basic plagiarism awareness); citation and plagiarism (citation as evidence of scope, critical engagement and disciplinary knowledge, quotation against paraphrase, trickier sources); and academic integrity (the six fundamental values, intentional and unintentional plagiarism, integrity as graduate and professional identity). It sits beside the sector's statements of integrity values and the information literacy models, which place citing within managing information. Its open questions are coverage at Introductory and Intermediate, the managing of sources it now carries, and which theory to link (Part E).

tierProgression.masteryNote: Across the tiers the weight moves along Anderson and Krathwohl's continuum, though not evenly: Introductory is declarative and procedural, what referencing is and how to do it, with keeping one's own records as the first metacognitive habit; Intermediate is procedural and strategic, quotation and paraphrase and citation used to show what one has done; Advanced returns to the conceptual, the values, and ends in the self-system, integrity as identity. The map builds from the concrete skill to the culminating "why", reversing the guide's order; in Marzano and Kendall's terms the learner moves from the cognitive system to the self-system, where values and identity direct conduct. Mastery is integrity as scholarly and professional practice, the map's Advanced goal, which is the core's A11 ladder from compliance to flow.

theorySpine.overview:
- Three tiers, Introductory, Intermediate and Advanced, each with a focus, content, a progression logic and links to other pathways (D:PTM, Pathway 4).
- Progression runs from referencing, to citation, to integrity: the reverse of the guide's chapter order (D:PTM, Pathway 4).
- Plagiarism threads through every tier: awareness at Introductory, avoidance through quotation and paraphrase at Intermediate, intentional and unintentional plagiarism at Advanced (D:PTM, Pathway 4; D:CARDS).
- Tiers are anchored to experience of the practice, not to year of study (D:TSPEC, section 2).
theorySpine.corePrinciples:
- Academic integrity is a literacy in its own right, made more pressing by essay mills and generative AI (D:EAU, p. 184).
- Learning is a journey from the edge of a discourse community, as a novice, towards its centre; integrity is part of the identity taken on along the way (D:EAU, p. 185).
- Academic integrity rests on six fundamental values: honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage (D:EAU, pp. 185-187, after D:ICAI).
- Integrity is more than avoiding plagiarism: the values inform conduct in professional contexts and graduate identity (D:EAU, p. 187).
- Referencing acknowledges where knowledge comes from, and is also a tool for meeting marking criteria (D:EAU, p. 188).
- Styles differ by discipline and by institution; the one required is checked in the module handbook or with the tutor, and used consistently and accurately (D:EAU, pp. 188-189).
- An in-text reference marks each use of a source; the references list gives every source used, in alphabetical order by author surname (D:EAU, pp. 189-191).
- Plagiarism is presenting another's words or ideas as one's own without acknowledgement; it is not always deliberate, but unintentional plagiarism comes from cutting corners, such as pasting text to reference later (D:EAU, p. 192).
- References show the reader the scope of the research and the engagement with the discourse; tutors often read the references list first (D:EAU, pp. 191-193).
- References signpost the critical edge and display disciplinary knowledge (D:EAU, pp. 192-193).
- Quotations should be kept to a minimum, because depending on them undermines the demonstration of understanding (D:EAU, pp. 193-194).
- Paraphrase restates a source's point in one's own words: identify the key point, disregard the rest, write it in your own words, and reference it (D:EAU, pp. 194-195).
- A references list contains only the sources cited; a bibliography also lists sources consulted (D:EAU, p. 196).
- Referencing's broader value is as the learner's means of demonstrating engagement with the relevant discourse (D:EAU, p. 6).
- Knowledge is the outcome of the interactions within a discipline's discourse community; a student joins that community and journeys from its periphery to its centre (D:EAU, pp. 29-30, after Lave and Wenger, 1991).
theorySpine.selection: Choose this pathway when the aim is to acknowledge sources accurately, use them without plagiarism, or act on integrity values. For finding and evaluating the sources, choose `path:finding-using-sources`, which hands over at the point a source is recorded; for using sources actively in an argument, `path:academic-writing` and `path:criticality`; for ethics in research with participants and data, `path:researching`; for integrity questions raised by AI tools, `path:ai-technology`. It suits badly a learner whose need is copyright or licensing in publishing or professional work, which it touches only through the values.

analysis: **The guide's vocabulary against the benchmarks':** the guide says referencing, in-text reference, references list, author-date or Harvard, quotation, paraphrase, plagiarism, intentional and unintentional, and the six ICAI values; the benchmarks say accurate referencing, standard systems, unethical behaviour, intellectual property, position of trust, professional attitude, respect for others' views. Both belong in the practice searcher's vocabulary for this pathway.
**Skill against theme:** five of the ten extracts are skill. Where integrity's words appear as themes they are word matches (trust in accounting topics) or concerns about generative AI.
**Book coverage:** Chapter 10 carries all nine cards, though the guide teaches integrity first and referencing after; the tier map reverses that order on purpose (its note on ordering).
**Other authors:** META holds Lave and Wenger only; Hyland, Howard and the ICAI framework are wanted (W-0029, W-0028, W-0026).

gaps.coreOpenQuestions:
1. **P2 triggers:** 4 and 5: every external framework was read by summary only, and Howard by recall (W-0016, W-0026 to W-0030). The crosswalk is editorial.
2. **Levels:** `unknown` for every capability (D-ing-0001 (a)).
3. **Capability coverage:** settled. Three capabilities added by the model's author (D-ing-0031 (a), Abbott, 01:41): c1 "Explain why academic work acknowledges the sources of its knowledge" (Introductory), which merges the model's "why we reference" into an explanation, worded formally at his request; c2 "Record and organise sources as they are found, so that every citation can be traced" (Introductory), SCONUL's Manage pillar (D-ing-0014 (a)), grounded in part in the guide (pp. 49, 186, 192, 196-198) and taught with SCONUL's model, which is cited as a source (Abbott, 01:45; ing N-0067); c3 "Use citation to show the scope of research and engagement with the discourse" (Intermediate, D:PTM, Pathway 4; D:EAU, pp. 191-193). Temporary ids until the model numbers them.
4. **Theory links:** settled (D-ing-0032 (a), Abbott, 01:48): the guide first, then Hyland (1999) as the key theory, queued at META's ing. [Amended by D-ing-0033, Abbott, 01:57: the guide stays out of the core's theory, as the source map rule requires (ing N-0012); Hyland (1999) is the key theory and Howard (1995) sits beside it, both queued at META's ing.] The guide's discourse community journey (pp. 29-30), which the guide draws from Lave and Wenger (1991), is linked to META's run 0033. Howard (1995) is referred to and mentioned; patchwriting may be explored at the Advanced tier beside Hyland [now a theory beside the key one, D-ing-0033]. The ICAI values are referred to in passing, with one or two of their key statements, and queued for ingestion because they recur in the AI and technology pathway. A9's targets and the capabilities' `theory:` fill in when the documents exist (W-0029, W-0028).
5. **The line with Researching:** the guide's chapter sets out research ethics and the ESRC's six principles (D:EAU, pp. 187-188); the model gives "ethics in the field" to Researching and keeps values and plagiarism here (D:PTM, Pathway 4). This document follows the model and records no research ethics content.
6. **The line with AI and technology:** the guide opens integrity with generative AI and essay mills (D:EAU, p. 184). The model places the AI integrity material in the AI and technology pathway as the AI-specific extension of this pathway's values and plagiarism content, to be cross-referenced, not duplicated (D:PTM, AI and technology pathway, cross-links). This document follows the model.
7. **The line with Academic Writing:** the referencing checks (citations matching the list, close paraphrase without a citation) sit in Academic Writing's four pillars self-review, pillar 4 (D-ing-0028, D-ing-0029); this pathway teaches the practice and the self-review checks it.
8. **Templates:** open. Proposed: a source log (stage 1); the paraphrase frame moved to Academic Writing (D-ing-0034). Offered to COMPOSE through META's ing when this document reaches `checked`, as for the other pathways.
9. **Order:** the model reverses the guide's order (A7a). Recorded, not questioned.
10. **Source map:** what *Excelling at University* teaches for each capability belongs in its guide map (held by `path`, draft), not here.
11. **Paraphrase:** settled (D-ing-0034 (b), Abbott, 02:00): putting a source into one's own words is a writing skill, taught in Academic Writing under its capability on integrating sources actively; this pathway keeps acknowledgement, so `referencing/02` narrows to "Avoid plagiarism by acknowledging quoted and paraphrased material correctly" (the model's to make; carried here as a proposal). Patchwriting stays at the Advanced tier as an integrity question, with Howard beside Hyland (D-ing-0033).
12. **Progression by level (A11):** drafted 02:36 (J-ing-0001; META D-0205; shape D-ing-0035, D-ing-0036). Every level was read by summary only (W-0031 to W-0034); the entries are editorial readings of the descriptors and the pathway's theory.
13. **Vocabulary (D-ing-0050, Abbott, 11:10):** swept. The guide's glossary terms for this pathway are in B2a (and A4 where new); candidates from the model's tier text are in B2b; A10's direct terms are the term list v1.0 patterns as words, with the ruled second version's changes noted. The search patterns themselves are kept with each consuming project, not here. No published glossary of this pathway's vocabulary has yet been read; B2b stays candidates.

usage.text: One SCORM course per tier, "Referencing, Citation & Academic Integrity: <Tier> Stage" (TN-1), from a shell and subject context packs (PKS-1).

usage.label: The first course
usage.text: `referencing-introductory` is the only course with a design run: Phase A ran once and is retired by RRN-1, to be rerun after the fixes in backlog 5.154. Its gate records are the place where this core's Introductory content first meets a design; whether the rerun has happened since `89ee9c4` is unchecked here.

usage.label: Referencing style is context, not shell
usage.text: The core teaches author-date as the worked style and sends the learner to the required one. In ADAPT the style belongs to the context pack's phase (PKS-1, Option B of 26 September; the RS-1 amendment puts it in the context definition), and references are to be stored as data and formatted for each context (`mta-ho-adp-prm-02`). The shell's content stays style-neutral where it can.

usage.label: Voice band
usage.text: Introductory, Intermediate and Advanced anchored to tier specification section 16, bands 2 to 4, default (`pathway-tier-mapping.md`, Pathway 4).

usage.label: Cross-links
usage.text: Supports Academic Writing (Pathway 6), whose four pillars self-review carries the referencing checks (pillar 4); research ethics in practice is Researching's (Pathway 9); integrity connects to the graduate identity thread in Pathway 1. The catalogue's `routes` are null, so the links live only in the prose.

usage.label: Benchmark mapping
usage.text: The 10 patterns are the word test for QV-TAG-2 part (e). `references` and `cite` are broad. `academic integrity` and `plagiaris*` will meet few subject benchmark statements, which treat integrity in general terms. Whether D-0028's v2 changes them is unchecked here.

usage.label: Practice connection and summative parity
usage.text: as for every pathway (D-0047; tier specification section 7).

openPoints: D-0058: the cards. Abbott added three at 01:41 (D-ing-0031 (a)): "Explain why academic work acknowledges the sources of its knowledge" and "Record and organise sources as they are found, so that every citation can be traced" (Introductory) and "Use citation to show the scope of research and engagement with the discourse" (Intermediate); for nts to land in `path` (ing N-0066).

The Manage pillar (D-ing-0014 (a)) is now a capability (c2). The guide grounds it in part (accuracy as honesty, the details each reference needs, efficient working, keeping a record while making notes); Abbott wants SCONUL's Seven Pillars model introduced in the lessons by name and cited in the course's sources (ing N-0067). This bears on `referencing-introductory`'s rerun (RRN-1) and its sources step (SIP-1).

The AI integrity material: the mapping puts it in Pathway 12 as the AI-specific extension of this pathway's values and plagiarism content, cross-referenced, not duplicated (`pathway-tier-mapping.md`, Pathway 12, cross-links). The two pathways' courses need to agree where each case sits.
Whether the catalogue's null `routes` should carry the mapping's cross-links.

Theory for the courses (D-ing-0033, 01:57, amending D-ing-0032 (a)): Hyland (1999) is the key theory and Howard (1995) sits beside it, with patchwriting possible at Advanced; the discourse community journey (Lave and Wenger, META run 0033) runs through the pathway; the ICAI values appear in passing. What the book teaches comes to the courses through its source map (`adp-ing-td-source-map-candidates-referencing.md` until `path` holds it). Hyland and the ICAI values are queued at META's ing (`adp-ing-ho-mta-ing-0007`), Howard by `adp-ing-ho-mta-ing-0008`.

Paraphrase (D-ing-0034 (b), 02:00): taught in the Academic Writing courses; the Referencing courses teach acknowledging quoted and paraphrased material and, at Advanced, patchwriting. `referencing/02` narrows accordingly; for nts to land in `path` (ing N-0072).

bookGrounding.chapters: Chapter 10 (Academic Integrity and Referencing, pp. 182-199), with discourse community and citation material elsewhere.

sections.teaches: Integrity as a literacy, made pressing by essay mills and generative AI
Defining academic integrity: the discourse community journey; the six ICAI values with examples; integrity as graduate identity
Research and the handling of data (Researching's ground)
Referencing styles; checking the handbook; consistency and accuracy
What references look like: in-text references and the references list
Why references matter: the ethical imperative, plagiarism, scope, the critical edge, disciplinary knowledge
Quotation and paraphrase (paraphrase now Academic Writing's, D-ing-0034)
Formatting references by source type; references list against bibliography
Referencing as the learner's way of showing engagement with the discourse; the discourse community
Exemplars: references showing engagement; numbered references in a science article; references integral to the discussion
Feedback flags referencing and integrity faults
